items.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007
items.q: my grandmother points to this old victrola and shows me how to wind it up, and there was this array — there was like two thousand old records... to an actual Louis Armstrong Okeh

ctx.x: Well I’m curious as to what — in your childhood or teen years or something — turned you on to the music from the twenties and thirties?

I actually started when I was like five years old. I was born in Brooklyn and raised out in Smithtown, Long Island. And my grandparents remained in Brooklyn and every holiday we would come and do holiday things — whether it was Mother’s Day, Thanksgiving, birthdays, Christmas, all that stuff. And they used to have a lot of parties in the twenties and thirties, family gatherings, where people brought old records, old phonograph records. They were married in 1922. And one day my grandmother points to this old…
And it was pop music at the time, right? Or not?

items.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007
items.q: I find a lot of inspiration, well, from a lot of those musicians: ... Armstrong

ctx.x: Did you start listening to it and sort of analyzing what you were hearing? You know, what kind of — was it a string bass, was this a — you know, what’s the instrumentation here? When did that come about for you?

Well on the early jazz recordings that my grandmother had there was definitely this sound that instrumentalists produced in those days that was a lost language as far as the fifties were concerned, particularly the way the saxophones would have that kind of little vibrato, that little moan, either hearing King Oliver or Louis Armstrong or some of the novelty cornetists. They had that kind of, you know, agitated vibrato. And there was a definite push on the downbeat, to get the thing going, and then this…
Were you able to enlist any of your friends?
